pins.name: Colonial Creek Campground Trailhead
pins.note: Drive-to trailhead in Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130; the Thunder Creek Trail leaves from the south end of the campground near the amphitheater. The alternative southern start is by boat to Stehekin and shuttle to High Bridge, then up the Park Creek Trail.
pins.directions: Drive SR-20 (the North Cascades Highway) to the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead, the start of the most commonly used approach into this basin. From there the Thunder Creek Trail — an easy, mostly forested stock and hiker trail — climbs only about 600 feet over its first 13 miles up-valley. Two alternate approaches reach the same high basin: a steeper, more direct line over McAlester Pass and down Rainbow Creek, also starting from SR-20, or a southern approach by boat or shuttle to Stehekin and High Bridge Camp, then up the Park Creek Trail. A North Cascades National Park wilderness permit is required, and if you're using the Stehekin ferry or shuttle, both run on a limited schedule — typically mid-June through September — so check timetables and reserve the permit before planning dates.

pins.name: Skagit Queen Camp
pins.note: Established camp near old Skagit Queen mine workings where the trail steepens into switchbacks; reliable creek water, common first- or second-night stop.
pins.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south from the Colonial Creek Campground trailhead on SR-20 — an easy, mostly-forested stock/hiker trail with only about 600 ft of gain — roughly 13 miles up-valley, passing McAllister Camp near mile 6 and Junction Camp near mile 9.5.

pins.name: Five Mile Camp, Park Creek trail
Park Creek Pass
pins.note: Trail high point in the notch between Mt. Logan and Mt. Buckner; camping is prohibited at the pass itself to protect fragile meadows, so continue on or camp just below it.
pins.directions: Continue up-valley past Thunder Basin Camp around mile 16.5, then pick up the signed Park Creek Pass Trail junction a couple of miles beyond; it switchbacks up through meadows to the pass.

pins.name: North-side exposed ledge traverse
pins.note: Class 3-4 ledge system traversing the backside of the summit towers, including a slight overhang requiring a squeeze-under move; most parties fix a line here.
pins.directions: From the cirque, ascend the long, very loose talus/scree slope on the path of least resistance toward the southwest gully system below the summit rocks, staying right of the horn-shaped rock gully at about 8,000 ft to be in the correct gully. This slope is the approach's main hazard — helmets on and space the party out for rockfall and unstable footing. Around 70 ft of Class 3 scrambling reaches the notch, and it is the right-most of the notches in the summit rocks; cross to the north side of it to gain the ledge.

pins.name: Summit crux crack
pins.note: 15-foot crack (Class 4 to low 5th) leads to the fixed rappel anchor used for the descent; rope up or belay through this section.
pins.directions: Traverse the ledge roughly 70 ft across the backside of the tower — two or three Class 4 moves, full exposure, and a squeeze under a slight overhang; many parties fix a line. The ledge widens and holds loose rock, so move carefully, then continue across the summit tower's backside to the small spur at the foot of the crack.

pins.name: Storm King summit
pins.directions: Climb the 15-ft solid Class 4 face crack, or wrap around its left side on easier Class 3 blocks; both reach the register and the fixed rappel slings. A final short Class 3 pitch tops out. Two points above 8,520 ft sit east of the triangulated 8,515 ft subsummit — the easternmost is the true high point.
